title: Data Visualization
text:
Welcome


This book takes a developmental approach to visualization motivating each new principle and chart element as a response to a limitation of what came before. The aim is to try to clearly visualize the underlying need rather than just learning rules of which charts are good for what. This is because I have noticed that learners can be apt at remembering that they should use one chart instead of another without understanding why that’s the case. Or they might understand why for a specific example, but not be able to generalize that understanding further.
I consider that helping learners understand and generalize is a way to empower their agency and improve their ability to predict what is an effective visualization choice for a visualization not previously encountered . At least it is my hope that this book can contribute to and encourage readers’ critical thinking about any chart they might come across. In my experience, this angle also makes learning more fun.
This books interleaves exercises throughout the chapters to encourage experiential learning and ignite readers intuition and make their learning more active. The exercises are largely focused on visualization principles rather than coding, since memorization of library APIs is an increasingly replaceable skill; although understanding the guiding principles of how those APIs are designed can be informative (e.g. the rules of a grammar of graphics library).
To make the learning interactive, the book also include code in a few libraries that implements a version of the grammar of graphics. I focus on these because I think they empower student in a similar way as described above: the predictable grammar encourages learners to interpolate what could work based on understanding the rules of the grammar.  

This books also hopes to introduce students to some interesting data sets along the way, although this will likely be a work in progress over a longer time.

title: 1  Why visualize data?
text:
1.1 What is data visualization?
At its core, data visualization is about representing data with graphical elements such as the position of a point, the length of a bar, or the color of a line. We usually visualize data for two main purposes: to improve own understanding of a dataset or to improve someone’s else’s understanding by communicating what we have learned. While we often use visualization to answer a specific question about a dataset, it can also be more exploratory and help us generate new questions.
In this sense, we can think of data visualization as a human “data language” that helps us gain and communicate data insights effectively. This role is equally relevant when an analysis comes from another person or from a machine, such as a generative AI agent: in either case, the goal is to support human understanding. By supporting both exploration and communication, visualization is often where a data analysis begins and ends.

title: 1  Why visualize data?
section: 1.9 Why are visuals easier to interpret than numbers?
text:
1.9 Why are visuals easier to interpret than numbers?
To understand why visualizations are so powerful, it is helpful to remember that to answer a question, we often have to put the data in a format that is easy for us humans to interpret. Because our number systems have only been around for about 5,000 years, we need to assert effort and train ourselves to recognize structure in numerical data.
On the other hand, visual systems have undergone refinement during 500,000,000 years of evolution, so we can instinctively recognize visual patterns and accurately estimate visual properties such as colors and distances without much conscious cognitive effort.
In practice, this means that we can arrive at correct conclusions faster by studying graphical rather than numerical representations of the same data.

A modern take on Anscombe’s quartet
For a more recent and dynamic illustration of how graphical representations are much easier for us to interpret, check out the Datasaurus Dozen animation below. It displays several different datasets, all with nearly the same mean, standard deviation and correlation between X and Y, but looking at the data graphically shows us how different these datasets actually are:






Figure 1.2: The Datasaurus Dozen: Datasets with near identical summary statistics but widely different distributions.



Now that you have experienced the benefits of visualizing data, let’s figure out how to create such visualizations!

title: 2  The grammar of graphics
text:
2.1 Why bother?
Why do we need to know anything about visualization libraries and their underlying theory, such as the grammar of graphics? While there is a lot we can learn about visualization without coding, the act of implementing visualizations in code can help us understand their underlying principles, which makes the learning experience more interactive and memorable. The grammar of graphics also gives us a powerful theoretical framework to understand and reason about data visualizations.

A helpful way to illustrate the difference between the two approaches to syntax is to imagine that we want to create a chart where we color the points according to their group. Here is pseudocode1 that illustrates this difference:

Imperative syntaxDeclarative syntax



fig = create_figure()
colors = ['blue', 'orange']
for color, group in zip(colors, df['group'].unique()):
    tmp_df = df[df['group'] == group]
    fig.add_chart(tmp_df['x'], tmp_df['y'], label=group, color=color)

Although the same chart is created from both of these pseudocode examples, the syntax looks wildly different. Pause here and try to describe the differences between the two in your own words. Then, click on the hint and solution below to read our explanation of the two approaches.
Actively engaging with exercises like this one can help you remember and understand the information. The key is to activate your brain and try to come up with an answer yourself rather than skipping straight to passively reading the solution.






Ex-hintHint






Does one of the approaches focus more on the data and the other more on the plot-specific details?






Ex-solutionSolution






Based on the syntax of the exercise above, we can say that a declarative approach to visualization lets us express ourselves in terms of the data (color='group'), whereas an imperative approach to visualization focuses more explicitly on plot construction details such as choosing specific colors and then assigning them to groups by looping through the data.












A related way to understand declarative and imperative approaches is to consider the difference between giving an instruction in each:

Declarative instructionImperative instruction



“Color by the column group in the dataframe.”
Focus: Declaring links between data variables (e.g., group) and graphical properties (e.g., color). The rest of the plot details (such as which colors to use) are handled automatically.




“Loop over the dataframe and plot observations in group a in blue and observations in group b in orange.”
Focus: Being explicit with all the details for creating the chart via loops and low-level drawing commands.




In this book, we will learn about declarative visualization tools, since these allow us to code a high-level specification of what we want the visualization to include, rather than coding out the details of how to implement the visualization. Another way to state this would be that high-level libraries let our minds focus on data and relationships, which is the right level of abstraction for a data scientist. Low-level libraries focus more on plot construction details, which is often more appropriate when making a highly customized visualization, data art, or an application with complex plotting logic.
Among declarative visualization libraries, there are still a few different subcategories. In this book, we are going to learn about libraries that implement a so-called “grammar of graphics”, since this framework makes visualizations easy both to create and to reason about.

title: 2  The grammar of graphics
section: 2.3 What is the grammar of graphics?
text:
2.3 What is the grammar of graphics?
There is a plethora of names used to refer to specific types of chart. While referring to charts by name can be convenient in some contexts, it is often confusing. For example, a scatterplot, a dot plot, a strip plot, a bubble plot, and a forest plot all use points to represent data, but what’s the difference between them? Memorizing exactly which chart corresponds to which name is not as important as developing an understanding of the principles that form the foundations for building visualizations. Such an understanding can move us away from just creating charts from known templates to reflecting on what it is we’re trying to communicate and which graphical elements are the most suitable for this task.
The grammar of graphics lets us focus on understanding the common building blocks of all charts and how to combine them according to predictable rules to create bespoke visualizations. It parallels the grammars of natural2 and programming languages, but applies to visual components. While we’re all familiar with how the grammatical rules of natural languages describe how to compose meaningful sentences from words, it might not be as clear what grammatical structures look like in programming languages, so let’s see an example in the following exercise:


Grammatical origins
The idea of a grammar of graphics originates from Leland Wilkinson’s book The Grammar of Graphics.







Ex-promptExercise 2






What do you think the output of the following Python code would be?


1 + 2

As you might have expected, the output is 3 because Python uses the conventional rules of mathematics to add the two numbers together. Almost all programming languages follow this rule. But what does the + operator do if we are trying to add something other than numbers? What do you think the output of the following code would be? Do you think it differs between programming languages?


'one' + 'two'








Ex-hintHint






Adding two numbers gives their sum. Could adding two strings similarly combine their contents, producing a string with all the characters from both?






Ex-solutionSolution






In Python, the + operator performs concatenation when strings are added together, so the returned result would be "onetwo". In contrast, R does not support adding strings with +, so it would raise an error indicating that non-numeric arguments were passed to the + operator.
This example illustrates that the same expression can behave differently under the grammatical rules of different programming languages.

title: 2  The grammar of graphics
text:
2.4 Learning the grammar of graphics
So what does the grammar of graphics look like? Well, “it depends”. Just like linguistic grammars vary between languages, visualization grammars are implemented differently in different packages. However, there are some core steps which are present in most grammars of graphics:

Create a data-linked canvas: This step creates a background canvas that other graphical components are drawn upon and links it to the relevant dataset.
Encode visual aesthetics: This step defines how data will be mapped to graphical channels (e.g., the column 'group' might be mapped to the color of each mark).
Add geometric marks: This step selects the graphical elements used to represent the data (e.g., points or bars).

As a result of the predictable structure, a grammar of graphics allows you to create an impressive range of visualizations in an intuitive manner and aids in reasoning about these visualizations. It also makes it notably easier to change between different types of plots, as the code syntax follows a predictable structure and only parts of the specification change between charts. In fact, libraries that implement a grammar of graphics often require fewer changes in the code to create different types of visualizations.3


Implementations of the grammar of graphics
You can think of the grammar of graphics as an underlying theory of how to make visualizations. But to actually create a visualization, we need to use a package that implements this theory in code. This book shows several programmatic implementations and lets you choose which package you prefer to learn, while also allowing for quick comparisons between libraries. Before creating a visualization, let’s see how the structure of these implementations is similar to the general structure we described above.

 Stellar naming
Altair is built on Vega-Lite, which in turn is built on the JavaScript visualization library Vega. Vega was named after a star and the name “Altair” was picked because it represents another star in the same astronomical pattern.




 A nod in the name
The “gg” in ggplot2 is a reference to Wilkinson’s The Grammar of Graphics, which inspired the creation of the ggplot2 library.

Altairggplot


In the Python package Altair, a general representation of the core chart components would look like this:

alt.Chart(data).encode().mark()

alt.Chart(data) creates the data-linked canvas.
encode(...) encodes the visual aesthetics, such as x and y.
mark_*(...) adds geometric marks, such as points or bars.


Note that we wrote the Altair syntax in the same form as in our general grammar of graphics example above to help you see how it maps onto that structure. It is perfectly fine to keep writing this way if you prefer it, but the canonical way to write Altair chart specifications is in the form alt.Chart(data).mark().encode(). We will follow that order from now on since most examples you will see elsewhere follow this syntax.



In the R library ggplot2, a general representation of the core chart components would look like this:

ggplot(data) + aes() + geom()

ggplot(data) creates the data-linked canvas.
aes(...) encodes the visual aesthetics, such as x and y.
geom_*(...) A geom function adds geometric marks, such as points or bars.


Note that we wrote the ggplot syntax in the same form as in our general grammar of graphics example above to help you see how it maps onto that structure. It is perfectly fine to keep writing this way if you prefer it, but the canonical way to write ggplot chart specifications is in the form ggplot(data, aes()) + geom(). We will follow that order from now on since most examples you will see elsewhere follow this syntax.

title: 3  Individual observations
text:
3.1 Why bother?
Plotting each individual observation separately is one of the most direct ways to visualize data. Rather than summarizing groups of observations, we’re simply putting one graphical point in our chart for every record in our table. As we saw in the introductory chapter, even this simple form of visualization can reveal patterns that are difficult to spot in a table of numbers.

Looking at the table above, we might start to generate questions about our data. Perhaps the cars with the best fuel efficiency are also the cars with the least powerful engines (i.e. do the cars with the highest Miles_per_Gallon also have the lowest Horsepower)? This sounds reasonable since a more powerful engine generally uses more fuel. Let’s see if we can answer this question with a visualization. To see how these two variables relate to each other, we can map them to two visual channels in the chart, such as x and y.

First, we create a canvas linked to the cars dataframe via alt.Chart(cars). Then, we indicate what kind of geometric mark we want to use to represent the data. Here, it is suitable to show the data as points using mark_point():

    x='Miles_per_Gallon',
    y='Horsepower'
)

 Different defaults
You can see that there are some differences in the default choices made by each library.
Different styles have different advantages, and they are easy to customize to look however you want, which we will learn about later.
Including the origin (x = 0, y = 0) or zooming in on the data can both be sensible defaults in different contexts, which we will also learn more about in later chapters.
Observations with missing values in either Miles_per_Gallon or Horsepower are omitted because they cannot be positioned on both axes. Some libraries explicitly warn about this and others don’t.
Does the chart answer our question? That’s up to you to explore in the exercise below!






Ex-promptExercise 1






Study the chart above. What can you say about the relationship between Horsepower and Miles_per_Gallon? If you choose to use statistical terms such as correlation, also explain them in plain English, as if you were explaining what the chart means to someone unfamiliar with statistics. Finally, it’s always good to ask yourself if your interpretation of the chart makes sense, given your knowledge about how the world works.






Ex-hintHint






It can be helpful to start with a particular area of the chart. For example, look at the cars with the most powerful engines (highest horsepower). What is their fuel efficiency? Now do the same for the cars with the least powerful engines and compare the two.

Horsepower vs Miles_per_Gallon
From the chart, we can see that Horsepower and Miles_per_Gallon are “negatively correlated”. In plain English, this means that cars with more powerful engines (higher Horsepower) tend to have lower fuel efficiency (lower Miles_per_Gallon). This makes sense, as more powerful engines often consume more fuel than less powerful ones. Note that we can’t make claims about a causal relationship from the chart alone, but in this case, the observed relationship in the chart supports our mechanistic understanding of the world.

title: 4  Magnitude
text:
4.1 Why bother?
In the last chapter, we saw how we could visualize magnitude as either the position of a point along an axis or as the brightness of the point’s color. We can refer to these different ways of representing a quantity graphically as visual “channels”. There are many more visual channels than position and brightness, and when we visualize something, we want to think about which are the most effective channels that we can use to understand the data.
As in many cases, an efficient way to learn this topic is through personal experience, rather than just being told the answer. So let’s experience how some visual channels are more effective than others through a short exercise.

title: 4  Magnitude
text:
Ex-promptExercise 1






Take a few seconds to answer the following question. How many times larger is the bigger object as the smaller one in each of these two images?




Remember that we learn more effectively when we actively try to answer questions like these instead of viewing the solution right away.






Ex-hintHint






What do you think is meant by “bigger” when it comes to the circles? Are you supposed to compare the areas or the diameters?






Ex-solutionSolution






The larger circle has seven times the area of the smaller circle, and the longer bar has seven times the length of the shorter bar.1



Most people find that it is much easier to compare the length and position of the bars aligned to the same baseline than to estimate the areas of the circles. For bars, it is also immediately clear what to compare as long as their widths are kept constant, whereas for the circles we might hesitate between area and diameter. This is important to keep in mind, especially when communicating to others via visualization, but also when creating plots for yourself.
Even if you aced both comparisons yourself, the fact that many people tend to get one of them wrong more often means that in order for you to create effective visualizations you need to know which visual channels are the easiest for humans to decode.

title: 4  Magnitude
text:
4.2 Visual channel effectiveness
There has been plenty of research trying to determine which visual channels are the most effective when communicating different aspects of a dataset. The findings from these studies provide us with a useful guiding foundation that we should only stray from with good reason. The main findings are summarized in the schematic below, from the most to the least effective visual channel.






Figure 4.1: Classical visual-channel ranking for quantitative magnitude judgments. Adapted from Visualization Analysis and Design, Tamara Munzner, with illustrations by Eamonn Maguire (2014, CC BY 4.0).





What is regarded as visually salient might vary across cultures, geographic regions, and age groups. This is important to remember since much of this research has been carried out with college students in North America and Europe. More recent studies have shown that the chart’s purpose and the combination of visual channels affect which ways of depicting magnitude are most effective.2
Position along a common scale is generally the most effective visual channel for precise magnitude comparisons, so we should use it for our most important comparisons when possible. In a scatterplot, for example, position along the x- and y-axes represents two variables, but we can also use size or color to represent additional variables. Although it is harder to judge exact quantities from these channels (is this dot’s area exactly twice that of another?), they can still help us see trends in the data.

Unnecessary 3D makes plot interpretation harder
Three-dimensional plots are especially problematic when the extra dimension serves only as decoration, as in a 3D bar or pie chart. Even when depth represents data, as in a 3D scatterplot, positions can be difficult to compare. This is particularly challenging in a static image on paper, where the reader cannot rotate the plot to inspect it from different angles.






Ex-promptExercise 2






Which value do you think is represented by the bar labelled “B” in the 3D bar chart below?









Ex-solutionSolution






The bars appear to have values of approximately A = 0.7, B = 1.7, C = 2.7, and D = 3.7, but this is an illusion caused by the viewing angle of the “camera” in this 3D scene. The actual values of A, B, C, and D are 1, 2, 3, and 4, respectively. This plot would have been much easier to read without the unnecessary 3D effect.










Meaningful 3D can facilitate plot interpretation
Sometimes 3D can be useful, such as in a topographic map or a visualization of a protein’s structure. Below you can see examples created with the rayshader library that use 3D representations and camera rotation to help us interpret spatial relationships. The example on the right visualizes the curvature of spacetime via 3D position (depth), eliminating the need for the additional 2D plot shown in the example on the left.




Video

Figure 4.2: A useful application of 3D.



But be cautious: we will see in the next section that even for systems such as blood vessels, which are naturally organized in three dimensions, it can be more mentally demanding to interpret a 3D visualization accurately. Claus Wilke has written a helpful chapter on this topic if you are interested in learning more.

title: 4  Magnitude
section: 4.3 Well-designed visualizations can support clinical decisions
text:
4.3 Well-designed visualizations can support clinical decisions
The importance of these best practices might seem a bit abstract until you experience their effects yourself. Let’s look at a concrete example of how changing visualization methods improved performance on a medically relevant task.
Heart disease is the most common cause of death, killing almost 9 million people each year, or as many as diabetes, dementia, neonatal conditions, and respiratory infections combined. Low wall shear stress—the frictional force per unit area exerted by blood on an artery wall— is associated with the development of atherosclerosis. Identifying these regions can therefore help clinicians assess areas at risk.
To evaluate the shear stress in the arteries, one approach is to use a digital 3D representation of the artery colored according to the magnitude of shear stress, which is what you can see in the picture below. The colormap changes from blue for the areas of interest (low stress) to cyan, green, yellow, and red for higher stress.
In a 2011 study, Michelle Borkin and colleagues tested how effective this type of visualization was compared to alternatives using 2D representations and a diverging color scale.3 The experiment involved 21 Harvard medical students, who were asked to identify regions of low shear stress. When using the visualization you see below, they correctly identified an average of ~40% of these regions.




Changing the color scale almost doubled the accuracy
One comparison tested the effect of changing the color scale to one that is easier to interpret and makes the important areas of low shear stress stand out more, by highlighting them in bright red and showing the remaining areas in shades of gray. With this seemingly small modification, the percentage of low-shear-stress regions correctly identified almost doubled, from 40% to 70% for the 3D representations.
We will talk more about choosing appropriate color scales in later chapters.





Changing from 3D to 2D improved accuracy further
Another comparison tested changing from a 3D representation of the blood vessels to a 2D representation while using the diverging color scale. Although a 3D representation preserves more of the vessels’ anatomical geometry, it is also more cognitively demanding for us to process, and some areas can cover others so it is harder to get a quick overview of the vessels. In the 2D visualization, the blood vessels and their branching points are shown in a schematic that is less cognitively demanding to interpret. This representation was also shown to be more effective, as 90% of the low-shear-stress regions were correctly identified on average.
Overall, these two changes more than doubled the percentage of regions correctly identified, from 40% to 90%. That is a huge increase from modifications that might have seemed to be merely a matter of taste without knowledge of visualization theory! So, if anyone tells you that visualization of data is not as important as other components, you can tell them about this study and ask them what kind of visualization they want their doctor to look at when analyzing their arteries.



As with many things, there are situations where you can depart from these guidelines if you are sure about what you are doing and are trying to create a specific effect in your communication. But most of the time, it is best to adhere to the principles discussed above and we will dive deeper into some of them later in the book.

title: 5  Groups
text:
5.1 Why grouping matters
So far, you have created declarative visualizations by representing observations as point marks on a canvas, using position and color to represent quantitative variables. This is the foundation for all the visualizations we will make, but it is rarely sufficient on its own to give a complete picture of the data. In particular, real-world datasets might show overall trends that disappear or change when individual groups are explored more closely. The goal of grouping is to distinguish between groups by basing the visual appearance or placement of points in a chart on the value of a categorical variable. Let’s see this in action in the following exercise.

title: 5  Groups
section: 5.2 The two main purposes of grouping
text:
5.2 The two main purposes of grouping
As we have seen in the exercises above, grouping can have major benefits. We can divide these benefits into two main categories, both of which help us arrive at more accurate conclusions about our data:


Directly compare observations between groups.
Reveal patterns within individual groups that are obscured when viewing the data from all groups together.


These benefits are often connected and can be explored simultaneously. When we grouped the alcohol consumption data by income level, the positive relationship in the pooled data was much less apparent within groups. Grouping also made it easier to compare observations between groups.

Simpson’s paradox
Differences between overall and within-group relationships are central to Simpson’s paradox (named after the statistician Edward H. Simpson, rather than the TV series). In the classic form of this phenomenon, a trend within individual groups reverses when the groups are combined. Grouping can also reveal trends that are weak or absent in the pooled data.
Below we show a simplified illustration of this aggregation effect. Notice how the overall dataset shows little apparent relationship between X and Y, but when the observations are colored by group, you can see that both groups exhibit a negative trend between X and Y: larger values of X tend to be associated with smaller values of Y, and vice versa. This is a prime example of the utility of grouping in deepening our understanding of a dataset; without it, we would have missed the within-group relationships.

title: 5  Groups
section: 5.3 What type of column can we use for grouping?
text:
5.3 What type of column can we use for grouping?
In general, we are interested in grouping data by “categorical” columns. If there is a natural order to the categories (e.g., education levels or letter grades), we can be more precise and call the column “ordinal”. If there is no such order, we say that the column is “nominal” (e.g., types of fruit or color names). As a general rule, we will not group data by quantitative columns that hold continuous data (e.g., height or age), but there are exceptions. For example, we might turn ages recorded in whole years into categories that we can group by, such as 18–24, 25–34, and 35–44.
 Don’t group data by quantitative columns that hold continuous data (e.g., height or age)

title: 5  Groups
text:
5.4 Channels for grouping
Generally speaking, position and color are the two most effective visual channels to use for grouping. Shape can also be used, but often either in combination with one of the other two or for a specific purpose.






Figure 5.2: Classical ordering of static identity channels for grouping; effectiveness depends on the task and design. Adapted from Visualization Analysis and Design, Tamara Munzner, with illustrations by Eamonn Maguire (2014, CC BY 4.0); motion omitted.



Let’s take a look at a familiar example: the traffic light. Do you think that traffic lights are well designed? At first glance, their use of red and green presents a challenge for people with red–green color vision deficiency. Thankfully, signals can communicate their meaning through position and shape as well as color, as in the pedestrian signals below.






Figure 5.3: Traffic lights often use color, shape, and position to communicate meaning. Pedestrian Vectors by Achmad Saroju via Vecteezy





Shape up
Some regions also use shape to distinguish traffic signals for cars, as in this example from Nova Scotia in eastern Canada.

Using several visual channels for the same distinction gives viewers more than one cue to interpret. Even traffic signals for cars that lack distinct shapes typically use a consistent arrangement, so drivers can use position as well as color to distinguish the signals.

Applying grouping strategies
The grammar of graphics allows for the grouping strategies to be conveniently defined via an easily interchangeable syntax:

Altairggplot




ColorShapePosition


encode(color='category_column')


encode(shape='category_column')


encode(x='category_column')
encode(y='category_column')








ColorShapePosition


aes(color = category_column)


aes(shape = category_column)


aes(x = category_column)
aes(y = category_column)









Color
The human brain can detect color differences with little cognitive effort. Color is a preattentive feature3 which means that the brain can tell apart colors even without conscious attention. This is heightened when there is a high contrast, such as between the complementary colors blue and orange.
This is great news for grouping! By encoding our categorical variable as color, we can leverage the brain’s ability to infer groups. Conveniently, color doesn’t alter the layout or structure of the data visualization, so it’s an efficient way to compare the exact values of data points between groups.
In the second exercise of this chapter, we already saw how color could be used to group our life expectancy data by income group. Let’s now see what the code to create this chart looks like:

Altairggplot


Here we use color='income_group':

import altair as alt
import pandas as pd


income_df = pd.read_csv('data/income_lifeexp_alcohol.csv')

alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group',
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






Here we use color = income_group:

library(tidyverse)

income_df <- read_csv('data/income_lifeexp_alcohol.csv')

ggplot(income_df, aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
        color = income_group
    )) +
    geom_point()

















WarningAvoid using color for more than 5–7 groups




Using too many colors or colors that are too similar can blur the differences between groups. There are also several other important aspects of using colors effectively, such as how to ensure accessibility, particularly for people with color vision deficiencies. We will learn more about these topics in a later chapter, but for now it’s enough to remember that when there are more than about 5–7 groups in the data, it might be better to break it down into separate charts instead of grouping by color.




Shape
Shape is a less effective grouping strategy on its own, but it can be combined with color to provide an additional visual cue.
The syntax for mapping a variable to the shape channel is similar to that for color:

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group',
    shape='income_group'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Setting filled=True fills all the points with a solid color, making the shapes easier to distinguish:

alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point(filled=True).encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group',
    shape='income_group'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
        color = income_group,
        shape = income_group
    ) +
    geom_point()











While this combined approach can make grouping clearer, there are some pitfalls. For instance, hollow symbols limit the total area that can be colored, reducing the impact of color. Filled shapes can make color easier to see when combining shape and color. Additionally, smaller shapes are difficult to distinguish, so when plotting a dense scatterplot of small marks, try restricting the number of unique shapes to three or fewer, or consider avoiding using shape altogether. 






WarningAvoid using color and shape for different variables



It is often difficult to interpret charts that map one variable to color and another to shape. This tends to lead to too much visual information and it is difficult to distinguish the many different combinations visually.
The many combinations of income group and region in this chart are hard to separate visually, which makes this chart ineffective: 

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point(filled=True).encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group',
    shape='region'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
        color = income_group,
        shape = region
    ) +
    geom_point()



















WarningAvoid using size to group by a categorical variable



Size is often used to represent the magnitude of quantitative data. Under limited circumstances, it can also be used for grouping data according to a categorical variable, but in general this is best avoided.
Since size has an inherent direction from small to large, it works better for ordinal than nominal categorical data. One example is the World Bank income levels, ranging from low to high. However, even when used for ordinal data, it is often difficult to tell different sizes apart, as you can see in the chart below.





  
  
  
  
  


  
  








Position

X and Y position
Grouping by position often creates the clearest separation between groups. Distributing the groups along the x- or y-axis gives each group its own visual lane, preventing observations from different groups from overlapping. However, the grouping column now occupies one positional visual channel, so there is only one positional channel left for encoding the values we want to compare between the groups.
Below, we distribute the regions along the y-axis. This leaves us with a choice of whether to use the x-axis for percentage_heavy_drinkers or life_expectancy_at_65. We cannot represent both quantitative variables with position in this chart.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='region',
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = region,
    ) +
    geom_point()

















WarningAvoid rotated category labels along the x-axis



We could swap the x and y variables above, but then the region labels would be rotated and harder to read. Short category labels that fit horizontally can work well on the x-axis. For longer labels, placing the categories on the y-axis usually makes the text easier to read.





  
  
  
  
  


  
  








Faceting
Faceting takes the concept of grouping to the next level. Instead of using different visual channels within a single chart, generates multiple charts (or “facets”), each dedicated to a grouped subset of the data. Faceting is particularly effective for highlighting distinct trends and patterns within each subset, as well as identifying extreme values or outliers within groups. We could think of faceting as a type of position grouping, but its advantage is that it keeps both the x- and y-axes free for other variables.
Let’s create a separate facet for each income group, so that the relationship between percentage_heavy_drinkers and life_expectancy_at_65 within each group stands out. We can lay out the facets differently depending on what we are most interested in comparing. If the y-axis is the primary channel for comparison, we would spread the facets out horizontally in a single row. If the x-axis is the primary channel for comparison, we would spread the facets out vertically in a single column. In either case, the scales should be shared for direct comparisons. Neither axis is our sole focus here: we are interested in comparing the overall pattern within each group, so we will lay out the facets in a compact grid to save space.

Altairggplot


To facet by income group, we can append .facet('income_group') to our chart. We create a 2 × 2 grid of facets by using the columns parameter.

alt.Chart(income_df, height=250, width=250).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
).facet(
    'income_group',
    columns=2
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




In addition to faceting on a single variable in the data, faceting can also be done over two variables: one spread horizontally and one spread out vertically in the faceted charts. In Altair, we would use the column and row parameters to achieve this. For example, to have facets that are grouped by both income group and region, we could use facet(column='income_group', row='region'). This can be effective when we need to group our data further, but it can make the chart difficult to take in at a glance, so it is best used when there are fewer categories in the faceting variables.


To facet by income group, we can add + facet_wrap(vars(income_group)) to our chart. The vars() function specifies which columns to use for faceting, just as aes() specifies the mappings from variables to visual channels.
By default, facet_wrap() arranges these four groups in a 2 × 2 grid, which is appropriate for our visualization. Here, we set the ncol argument explicitly to illustrate how you can control the number of columns in the facet grid.

ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65
    ) +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(vars(income_group), ncol = 2)








In addition to faceting on a single variable in the data, faceting can also be done over two variables: one spread horizontally and one spread out vertically in the faceted charts. In ggplot, we would replace facet_wrap() with facet_grid() to do this. For example, to have facets that are grouped by both income group and region, we could use facet_grid(rows = vars(region), cols = vars(income_group)). This can be effective when we need to group our data further, but it can make the chart difficult to take in at a glance, so it is best used when there are fewer categories in the faceting variables.



As you can see above, faceting makes it easier to observe the overall pattern for each income group and how tightly clustered the values are. It also reveals potential outliers in the upper-middle-income facet: we can easily spot two countries with a higher percentage of heavy drinkers than the others in that group. On the other hand, it is now harder to compare individual values between groups because the points are spread across different charts instead of being close together in a single chart.
All the previous grouping strategies can be used within each facet as additional layers of grouping. This nested grouping can be useful for dividing our data according to multiple categorical variables, but it can become confusing if we try to fit too much into a single visualization. How many grouping variables you can use depends on how well separated the groups are and how many observations you have. More observations and less separation between groups mean that you need to be more careful and may need fewer layers of grouping to keep the visualization easy to interpret.
Let’s try out an example of how we can use faceting together with other grouping strategies.






Ex-promptExercise 3






Edit this chart to use both faceting and color for grouping. Facet by world region (region) and color the points by World Bank income group (income_group). Ensure that only two facets are shown per row.

Altairggplot



































Ex-solutionSolution







Altairggplot



alt.Chart(income_df).mark_point().encode(
    x='percentage_heavy_drinkers',
    y='life_expectancy_at_65',
    color='income_group'
).facet(
    'region',
    columns=2
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(income_df) +
    aes(
        x = percentage_heavy_drinkers,
        y = life_expectancy_at_65,
        color = income_group
    ) +
    geom_point() +
    facet_wrap(vars(region), ncol = 2)

title: 6  Order
text:
6.1 Why order matters
In Chapter 5, we learned how to distinguish groups of observations. Now we will look at observations that also have a meaningful order, such as time of day or an increasing dose of a treatment. In the following exercise, we will see how the grouping strategies we learned previously can be effectively complemented when working with ordered data.

title: 6  Order
text:
Ex-promptExercise 1






In the chart below, we can see how CO₂ emissions per capita have changed over time for the world’s continents. As you can see, the chart applies the strategies we have learned so far and uses color to group observations from different continents. But the overlap between the different groups makes it difficult to follow changes over time for any particular continent, and the chart is a bit confusing even after studying it for a while. How do you think you could change this chart to make it easier to see how CO₂ emissions per capita for each continent have changed over time?





  
  
  
  
  


  
  










Ex-hintHint






Do you think connecting the points belonging to the same continent would make it easier or harder to spot trends?






Ex-solutionSolution






We can use the natural order of the observations to connect the points that belong to the same continent with a line. Drawing a line from the earliest to the most recent year helps us with two things: it makes it easier to see changes over time for any single continent, and it makes it easier to see which points belong to which continent. As such, a line is a graphical tool that assists with both ordering and grouping.

points.mark_line() + points.mark_point(filled=True, strokeOpacity=1)

To explore how to create line charts, we will visualize population and fertility estimates at eight-year intervals from 1850 to 2018. The data comes from the Gapminder country-level dataset, and has been adapted for this textbook.
