When reading in a new dataset, it is always a good idea to have a look at a few rows as we did above, to get an idea of what the data looks like.
The world dataset has one row per sampled year, with the total population of the countries in the source dataset and the average of their fertility estimates (children_per_woman). Fertility here estimates the number of children a woman would have over her lifetime if the year’s age-specific birth rates persisted; it is not the number born per woman in a single year. Each country contributes equally to the average in our table, so this is a country average rather than a population-weighted global estimate. The regional dataset, which we will use later, applies the same summaries within each region.
Since the data reaches all the way back to the 1850s, it would be really interesting to plot how the world population grew over the period covered by the data. We can use a line plot to show this change over time.






Ex-promptExercise 2






Sketch the visualization (by hand is better than in your mind, which is better than nothing…) so that it is clear what you expect the plot to look like before continuing.






Ex-solutionSolution






If we sketched this visualization on paper, we might expect something like this: a single line that rises from the 1800s to the end of our dataset as the population increases.














Drawing of estimated world population growthNow we are ready to create our plot! By convention, time variables such as year tend to be laid out along the x-axis, while quantitative measures such as population tend to occupy the y-axis.

Altairggplot


In Altair, we use mark_line() to connect observations with a line.

alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x='year',
    y='population'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




You can see that the formatting on the x-axis includes a comma as a thousands separator. While this is desirable for regular quantitative variables, it is not how we are used to seeing years displayed. To deal with this, we can either change the underlying data type or the number formatting of the axis.
To change the axis formatting, we need to leverage the helper class alt.X (similar helpers exist for other channels, such as alt.Y and alt.Color). These classes help us customize many aspects of our charts. When using just x='year', we’re using shorthand for alt.X('year'); we just save ourselves some typing.
Here we are going to set alt.X('year').axis(format='d'), where the d is short for “decimal integer” (i.e., a base-10 integer).

alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='population'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Now the years are formatted as we are used to seeing them!


In ggplot, we use geom_line() to connect observations with a line.

ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = population)) +
    geom_line()













 Population plateau
Although the historical curve might suggest that the population will keep growing rapidly, the UN’s 2024 projections suggest a peak of around 10.3 billion people before the end of the century, followed by a gradual decline.
Interestingly, the line in this example helps us notice a change in the slope. The world population increased more slowly in absolute numbers before around 1950, and more rapidly afterwards.
After making any chart, it’s beneficial to ask yourself: “Is this what I expected to see from the data?” and “Does what I’m seeing make sense with what I know about this topic?” If we think about what happened in the world around the time of the change in the population growth dynamics, a major event that stands out was the end of World War II in 1945. It seems reasonable that transitioning from a war involving many countries around the world to a time of peace and increased safety could lead to an increase in the number of babies born. Let’s explore whether the timing of the change coincides with an increase in our country-average fertility measure.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='children_per_woman'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = children_per_woman)) +
    geom_line()











The country-average fertility estimate does show a rise from the late 1930s to the early 1960s, followed by a decline. This “explosion” is what is commonly referred to as the “baby boom”. However, remember that this chart averages country-level fertility estimates rather than taking the population in each country into account, so it does not directly show the total number of babies born in the world.






Deep-diveDeep dive






One more important piece of the puzzle here would be to look at life expectancy data to see if people were also living longer lives during this period, which would also contribute to population growth. Historical life expectancy estimates vary in coverage and reliability, but you can explore available estimates at Our World in Data.










WarningAvoid claiming causation from visualizations alone



You might have heard that “correlation is not causation”, and that applies here too. Although the end of World War II seems like a plausible contributor to some of the trends we have explored, it is important to understand that plausibility alone does not establish the cause of the observed patterns. Usually, several contributing factors interact to produce a more complex picture. This article about the baby boom elaborates on what we explored here. Among other things, it notes that many countries saw birth rates begin to rise even before World War II.

title: 6  Order
text:
6.3 Combining lines and points
Generally, it is helpful to add points on top of a line to indicate exactly where each observation from the data lies.

Altairggplot


In Altair, we combine lines and points through a concept called layering, where charts are superimposed on each other. The + operator means to “layer” a chart on top of another chart.  

line = alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='children_per_woman'
)
line + line.mark_point(filled=True)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Each basic Altair chart specification uses a single mark type, so line.mark_point() replaces the line mark with a point mark in the chart that we are layering on top of our original. 


In ggplot, we combine lines and points through a concept called layering, where charts (or “graphical layers”) are superimposed on each other. The + operator means to “layer” a geom on top of another geom.

ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = children_per_woman)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point()











This highlights something important: what does the line between the data points mean? Let’s find out in the next exercise.






Ex-promptExercise 3






In our data, there are only observations from every eighth year, but the line we have drawn is continuous and has a defined value for children_per_woman even between the points in the chart. For example, in this zoomed-in view we can see that the line at the year 1950 suggests a country-average fertility estimate of approximately 5.4 children per woman. But as we can see from the points in the chart, our data does not contain any observation from exactly the year 1950. What conclusions can we draw about the fertility estimate for this year?





  
  
  
  
  


  
  










Ex-hintHint






Think about the purpose of the line: is it just a visual aid, or does it represent any feature of the underlying data?






Ex-solutionSolution






The line segments between two observations are there to guide the eye; they do not establish what the values are at every unobserved moment between two points. Although the line is a simple linear interpolation between observations, which might seem harmless, it is important to consider whether the distance between two points represents a long enough period that important changes could be hidden by a straight line. To understand this more deeply, we can look at what would happen if the observations were closer or farther apart in time, as in the chart below.





  
  
  
  
  


  
  




As you can see, drawing a line between the observations sampled 20 years apart misses the rise in the average fertility estimate: it decreased until around 1940, then increased until around 1960, after which it started to decrease again.
How closely observations need to be spaced for straight connecting lines to be a useful approximation depends on which question we are asking. For example, if we are interested in exploring seasonal variation within each year, then even a chart with one observation every year would be insufficient. We would need more frequent observations, such as monthly values.


















WarningAvoid connecting unordered categories with a line



As we just saw, we need to be careful when interpreting a line between two observations along a quantitative axis. For the same reason, we should generally avoid using a line to connect observations along an axis of unordered categories. Here are two representations of the same population values:





  
  
  
  
  


  
  




The chart to the left is easy to interpret; it shows how many people lived on each continent in 2018, with a point for each continent’s value. But what about the line chart to the right? What does it mean that the line is at 1,000 million as it goes from Africa to Europe? That 1,000 million people lived somewhere between Europe and Africa? No, in contrast to how a line connecting two quantitative values can hint at what the value between them might have been, there is no meaningful numerical interval between these unordered categories, and therefore lines should generally not be used to connect observations across them.








Deep-diveDeep dive






Sometimes we want to show how the relationship between two quantitative variables has changed over time. We can do this by plotting the two variables of interest on the x- and y-axes, then connecting the points in chronological order.

Altairggplot


The order encoding controls the order in which observations will be connected by a line. Since there is no visible axis for the year, it would be difficult to know in which direction to read the chart; is the most recent year represented by the point in the top-left or bottom-right corner? To avoid this confusion, we add a tooltip so that you can see which year each point corresponds to when hovering over it with the mouse pointer.

line = alt.Chart(world).mark_line().encode(
    x='children_per_woman',
    y='population',
    order='year',
    # Display the numeric year as an integer without a thousands separator
    tooltip=alt.Tooltip('year', format='d')
)
line + line.mark_point(filled=True)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






By default, geom_line() connects points in the order of the variable on the x-axis. To connect points in another order, we can use geom_path() instead. This geom connects observations in dataframe row order, so we need to make sure our data is sorted by the variable we want the connection order to represent.
Since there is no visible axis for the year, it would be difficult to know in which direction to read the chart; is the most recent year represented by the point in the top-left or bottom-right corner? To avoid this confusion, we add a text label so that you can identify the earliest and most recent observations.

endpoints <- world |>
  filter(year %in% range(year, na.rm = TRUE))
ggplot(world |> arrange(year), aes(x = children_per_woman, y = population, label = year)) +
    geom_path() +
    geom_point() +
    geom_text(
        data = endpoints,
        vjust = -0.5  # Move the labels above the points to avoid overlap
    )











So how do we read this chart? We start by finding the year corresponding to the earliest observation; in this case, it is at the bottom right of the chart. Then we can follow the progression of the relationship between the world’s population and the country-average fertility estimate over time (i.e. towards the top left corner). The horizontal space between two points corresponds to the change in the country-average fertility estimate, whereas the vertical space corresponds to the change in the world population between those two years. If the points are close together, the changes were small relative to the displayed axis scales; points farther apart indicate larger changes on those scales.

title: 6  Order
text:
6.4 Areas and multiple ordered groups
Another way of representing ordered data is to fill the area between a line and a baseline.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(world).mark_area().encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='population'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(world, aes(x = year, y = population)) +
    geom_area()











Both lines and areas preserve the sequence of values over time. Filling the area down to a zero baseline emphasizes the magnitude of those values, while a line emphasizes the path through them. When displaying multiple ordered groups, lines and areas have different advantages, which we will learn about in this exercise.






Ex-promptExercise 4






We now use the regions dataframe, which contains a separate population value for each region in each year. Region determines which observations belong to the same group, and year determines their order within that group.

Altairggplot


Setting color applies to both areas and lines; if we wanted to control them individually, we could instead use stroke (for lines) and fill (for areas). Here we also use the | layout operator to position the plots next to each other horizontally (& lays them out vertically instead; we will learn more about layouts in a later chapter).

regions = pd.read_csv('data/gapminder_regions_from_1850.csv')

base = alt.Chart(regions, width=150, height=150).encode(
    x=alt.X('year').axis(format='d'),
    y='population',
    color='region'
)
base.mark_area() | base.mark_line()




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






geom_area() stacks the regional areas by default. The population values are already in the dataset, so we can map them directly to the y-axis. To set the area color, we use the fill aesthetic, whereas the line color is controlled by the color aesthetic. We map both to region.  Here we also use the | layout operator from the patchwork library to position the plots next to each other horizontally (/ lays them out vertically instead; we will learn more about layouts in a later chapter).

library(patchwork)

regions <- read_csv('data/gapminder_regions_from_1850.csv')

base <- ggplot(regions, aes(x = year, y = population, fill = region, color = region))
base + geom_area(show.legend = FALSE) | base + geom_line()











For each of these three questions, which chart is most appropriate?

How has the world population changed over time?
How has the population of the Americas changed over time?
Which region had the second-highest population in 2018?







Ex-hintHint






Note how the areas are stacked on top of each other, whereas the lines are not. Which chart makes the total easiest to read? Which lets you compare regional values against a shared baseline?






Ex-solutionSolution







The area chart makes it easiest to see how the total world population has changed over time, as we can read this value directly off the y-axis since the areas are stacked on top of each other.
Using a line chart is the preferred choice when we want to focus on comparing groups, either exact individual observations or the progression over time, rather than the total of the groups added together. From the stacked colored regions, we also get a rough idea of how each region has grown, but it is hard to make exact comparisons, because most regions do not share a baseline. The drawback of a line chart is that it’s quite cognitively demanding to try to reconstruct the total world population by adding all the lines up together, especially over time!
For the same reasons as in (2), a line chart makes it easier to see that Africa had the second-highest population in 2018, behind Asia. The sampled values show Africa below the Americas in 1994 and above it in 2002.



















WarningAvoid layering areas and stacking lines



While it might initially seem that overlapping areas instead of stacking them could remedy some of the issues mentioned above, the filled regions can obscure one another, as you can see below (there are a few exceptions such as density plots which we will see in a later chapter).





  
  
  
  
  


  
  




Similarly, stacked lines are usually difficult to interpret: each line’s height represents a cumulative sum rather than its own group’s value. If the sum is meaningful, use an area chart instead.








WarningAvoid stacking areas when summing groups is nonsensical



Avoid stacked area charts when the sum of the different groups in the chart is not meaningful, since stacking effectively sums the area heights together. For example, if we wanted to know the average number of children per woman around the world, stacking areas does not make sense since this adds the regional averages rather than calculating an overall average. Reading the y-axis of the stacked areas thus becomes misleading and confusing; the world average wasn’t 30 children per woman in the 1800s…

title: 7  Summaries
text:
7.1 Why bother?
In Chapter 6, we connected observations to make their sequence clear. Sometimes, however, our question concerns a collection of observations: How many are there? What is their total? What is a typical value? A summary helps answer these questions by reducing many values to a few. In this chapter, we will explore how to reduce a collection of observations to useful quantities.
That reduction is useful, but it also leaves information out. As we work through this chapter, keep asking: What did we lose, and how much of it do we need to put back? We will explore these questions here and in the following chapters.

title: 7  Summaries
text:
Ex-promptExercise 1







Suppose you are interested in whether meditation could help you feel less stressed before your next exam. The dataset below is a 500-observation sample from a randomized study.1 It contains stress scores from four meditation conditions and a control condition in which participants listened to a story excerpt. The stress score averages 20 items from a questionnaire where each item ranges from 1 to 4, with higher scores indicating greater self-reported distress after the activity.
How do the recorded stress scores differ between conditions? We start by applying the strategies we have learned so far: grouping observations by position and comparing their values on a shared scale.

Altairggplot



import pandas as pd
import altair as alt

meditation = pd.read_csv('data/meditation-stress-sample.csv')

alt.Chart(meditation).mark_point().encode(
    y='condition',
    x='stress'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

meditation <- read_csv('data/meditation-stress-sample.csv')
ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition, x = stress)) +
    geom_point()











What conclusions can you draw?






Ex-hintHint






Can you tell where most observations lie in each condition? Could several observations share the same position in the chart?






Ex-solutionSolution






Although we followed the strategies we have learned so far, overlapping points make it difficult to compare where observations are concentrated. We can see the range of recorded scores, but not how many observations share each position. Read on to find out how we could make these comparisons easier.

title: 7  Summaries
text:
7.2 Visualizing statistical summaries
In Chapter 1, we saw that statistical summaries can make some patterns easier to identify than they are in a raw table of numbers. We can use a similar strategy here by comparing the mean stress score in each condition.

Altairggplot


In Altair, we can write a supported aggregation function such as mean, median, or sum directly as a string wrapping the column name, for example, 'mean(stress)':

alt.Chart(meditation).mark_point().encode(
    y='condition',
    x='mean(stress)'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






In ggplot, we can tell geom_point() to use a summary statistic instead of the individual observation values. We set stat = 'summary' and specify a function that returns a single value, such as mean, median, or sum. For geom_point(), the default stat is 'identity', which uses the supplied values directly; other geoms can have different defaults.

ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition, x = stress)) +
    geom_point(stat = 'summary', fun = mean)








Instead of calling geom_point() and setting the stat parameter, we could call stat_summary() and set the geom parameter:

ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition, x = stress)) +
    stat_summary(geom = 'point', fun = mean)

These two calls produce the same chart, and both are commonly used. Sticking with the geom_ approach makes the code syntax more consistent, whether we are plotting individual observations or summaries. This Stack Overflow answer explains the relationship between geoms and stats in more detail.





 Should the axis include zero?
As you can see, different packages make different decisions about whether to include zero by default. For point summaries, the appropriate axis range depends on the comparisons we want to make and the meaning of the scale. We will discuss axis limits in more detail later.
Now we can clearly see that on average there are some differences between the groups.

title: 7  Summaries
text:
7.3 Visualizing spread
But showing only the mean hides the variability in the observations. How the individual values are distributed also affects the conclusions we can draw from the data.
So, whenever we show a measure of central tendency such as the mean or median, it is helpful to pair it with an indication of the underlying variability.
Here, we need to distinguish two concepts: the spread of the underlying data (descriptive statistics) and the uncertainty in the estimate of central tendency (inferential statistics). These answer two different questions, but graphically they are often depicted similarly. In this chapter, we will focus on how spread out the underlying data distribution is, and return to confidence intervals and other measures of inferential uncertainty in a future chapter.  
One measure of the spread in the underlying data is the standard deviation, which measures how spread out observations are around the mean.2 Let’s see how we can include the standard deviation together with the mean in our charts:

Altairggplot


The errorbar mark allows us to plot several common measures of variability, including an interval from one standard deviation below the mean to one above it. We’re changing the color of the point marks to match the error bar. We are using mark_circle as a shortcut for mark_point(filled=True). The point layer calculates the mean, while the error-bar layer calculates its interval from the individual stress scores.

base = alt.Chart(meditation).encode(
    y='condition',
    x='stress'
)
points = base.mark_circle(color='black').encode(x='mean(stress)')

points + base.mark_errorbar(extent='stdev', color='black')




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






As the name implies, the pointrange geom creates both a point and a range. Previously, we passed a summary function to the fun parameter. Here, we use fun.data because we need a central value and the lower and upper endpoints of the interval. Whereas fun accepts functions that return a single value, such as mean, fun.data accepts functions that return a dataframe with the summary and interval endpoints. In this horizontal chart, those values determine positions along the x-axis.
The fun.args parameter looks a bit cryptic. What it does is to pass mult = 1 (multiplier) to the mean_sdl function, which otherwise multiplies the standard deviation by 2 by default.

ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition, x = stress)) +
    geom_pointrange(stat = 'summary', fun.data = mean_sdl, fun.args = list(mult = 1))








The mean_sdl() function requires the Hmisc package. If it is missing, ggplot may report a failed statistical computation and omit the layer; check the rendering messages if the summary does not appear.



This gives us some additional information: we can see that all the conditions had a similar spread in the underlying data. While pairing a mean with an indication of its standard deviation is better than just showing a mean alone, it can still hide important features of the data. As we learned in the first chapter, statistical summaries don’t tell the whole story, even when we plot them. Let’s explore that more in this exercise.






Ex-promptExercise 2






To the left, we can see the mean ± one standard deviation for two groups of observations. To the right, there are four different suggestions for what these underlying observations might look like. By studying this chart, which sets of possible underlying observations do you think could produce the summary chart on the left?







  
  
  
  
  


  
  













Ex-hintHint






It’s more than just one of them…






Ex-solutionSolution






In this case, all four scenarios produce the same means and standard deviations for groups A and B! If you only look at the mean ± SD chart, you cannot tell which of these very different datasets it represents. This matters because depending on what your observations look like, you will come to different conclusions. For example, an outlier might be a genuine observation or a measurement error. Seeing it lets us investigate its origin and its influence on the summary. Or what if group A follows a symmetric distribution whereas group B shows a bimodal spread?
Note that in the case of the bimodal distribution of observations we should ask ourselves whether it is at all useful to include a mean. Maybe we should omit it here, since few of the observations are actually close to the mean and the mean therefore does not tell us much about the underlying observations. In this case, it may be more helpful to talk about the two clusters instead of trying to represent all the observations with a single average value. 












Figure 7.1: Underlying distributions for mean and standard deviation. Adapted from Beyond bar and line graphs.

title: 7  Summaries
text:
7.4 Including the underlying observations
To avoid being misled by a lone summary statistic, we can show the underlying observations of each group together with the statistical summaries. Plotting every observation in a group along the same line can lead to overlap. Jittering adds small random offsets to the points to help separate them. Here, we jitter only along the categorical y-axis, so each point’s horizontal position still represents its recorded stress score.


Jitterbug
Back in the 1930s, the jitterbug was a lively, often wild, dance style that matched the fast-paced, unpredictable energy of swing music. In data visualization, jittering serves a similar purpose: to add a touch of randomness to points in a plot.


Altairggplot


We calculate a random value for each observation and use yOffset to spread the points within each condition’s row. We then layer the mean and standard deviation interval over those points.

base = alt.Chart(meditation, height=alt.Step(30)).encode(
    y=alt.Y('condition').scale(padding=0.4),
    x='stress'
)

points = (
    base
    .transform_calculate(jitter=alt.expr.random())
    .mark_circle(color='lightgrey')
    .encode(
        yOffset=alt.YOffset('jitter:Q'),
        x='stress'
    )
)

points + base.mark_errorbar(extent='stdev', thickness=1.5) + base.mark_circle(size=40, color='black').encode(x='mean(stress)')




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition, x = stress)) +
    geom_point(position = 'jitter', color = 'grey') +
    geom_pointrange(stat = 'summary', fun.data = mean_sdl, fun.args = list(mult = 1))








As a shortcut for jittered points you could also use the specialized geom geom_jitter().

title: 7  Summaries
text:
7.5 Showing medians with boxplots
What if we visualize the median instead of the mean? Showing the median can be especially useful when there are a few extreme values in the data since these impact the mean more than the median, and the median thus becomes a more helpful indication of a typical value. But this decision is context-dependent: if we are interested in these extreme values, the mean may capture their influence in a way that is relevant to our question. Therefore, it is often a good idea to show means and medians together, since they tell us different things about the data.
A common measure of spread used together with medians is a percentile interval, which marks the range between two chosen percentiles. For comparison, the interval from one standard deviation below the mean to one above it contains about 68% of a normal distribution.
A common way to show the median and a percentile interval is a boxplot. The box spans the 25th to the 75th percentile, enclosing the middle 50% of the data, with a line marking the median. In the default boxplots below, the whiskers extend to the most extreme observations within 1.5 interquartile ranges of the box edges; observations beyond the whiskers are drawn separately. This illustration can help you interpret the different parts of the box:






Figure 7.2: The elements of a boxplot.




Altairggplot



alt.Chart(meditation).mark_boxplot().encode(
    y='condition',
    x='stress'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition, x = stress)) +
    geom_boxplot()











Although boxplots show multiple percentiles, they still hide important information about the underlying observations and should therefore also ideally be used together with a plot of the underlying observations or as a concise summary of the data after having inspected the underlying observations ourselves.






Figure 7.3: This illustration from Autodesk Research shows how boxplots can look the same even when the distribution of the underlying observations changes drastically.









WarningAvoid drawing conclusions from summary charts alone



Summary charts such as mean ± SD plots and boxplots are useful since aggregation reduces the complexity of the chart. But even if you are interested in comparing group summaries such as means or medians, you should always also inspect the underlying observations to understand how they are distributed and whether there are any outliers, since this affects the conclusions you can draw from the chart.

title: 7  Summaries
section: 7.6 What conclusions can we draw from the data?
text:
7.6 What conclusions can we draw from the data?
The charts show differences in recorded stress scores between conditions in this sample. However, we have not assessed the statistical significance of those differences. Standard deviations and boxplots describe the spread of the observations, not the uncertainty in the group means or their differences. In particular, overlap between these descriptive intervals does not establish whether a difference is statistically significant. That would require an appropriate inferential analysis, informed by the study design.
What about the magnitude of the differences? In this dataset, the meditation conditions have mean stress scores about 0.14–0.28 units below the story-listening control condition. Is that a lot or a little? These are differences on the 1–4 questionnaire scale described above; judging their practical importance also requires considering what difference would matter in this context. The charts help us describe the sample, but they do not by themselves establish that meditation caused the differences or that the differences are large enough to matter in practice.
The original study’s main analysis, using 2,239 participants across 37 sites, found evidence that all four 15-minute mindfulness exercises reduced self-reported stress relative to the active control. The largest mean difference was for body scan: 0.27 points lower than the control on the 1–4 scale. The authors concluded that even these brief exercises can offer modest, short-term benefits.

title: 7  Summaries
text:
Sparacio et al. (2024), Self-administered mindfulness interventions reduce stress in a large, randomized controlled multi-site study, Nature Human Behaviour, 8, 1716–1725.↩︎
The population standard deviation is the root mean squared deviation from the population mean.↩︎

title: 8  Counts & proportions
text:
8.1 Counts
In Chapter 7, we explored central values and variability. Another useful summary is the number of observations in a group. We will return to the meditation dataset to compare counts across conditions, then explore proportions and different ways to show parts of a whole.
We can summarize the number of observations in each group by computing a count.
When we are showing an accumulated value like a count or sum, it can be beneficial to replace our point mark with a bar to be able to more clearly compare groups. Bar charts visualize magnitudes as position and length. Since the bar is drawn from zero, it makes the accumulated amount explicit through its length (you can think of the bar as representing all the individual observations stacked on top of each other).

title: 8  Counts & proportions
text:
Altairggplot


We can use the 'count()' aggregation to count observations. By default, the categories are sorted alphabetically from top to bottom on the y-axis.

alt.Chart(meditation).mark_point().encode(
    x='count()',
    y='condition'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






We can use stat = 'count' to count observations. This stat computes the counts itself, so we don’t need to supply a summary function such as mean or median. By default, the categories are sorted alphabetically from bottom to top on the y-axis.

ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition)) +
    geom_point(stat = 'count')













Altairggplot



alt.Chart(meditation).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()',
    y='condition'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






To discourage the use of bars for summaries, the default for geom_bar is stat = 'count', which means we can write just geom_bar().

ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition)) +
    geom_bar()








Note that we have reduced the figure height so that the horizontal bars have a reasonable thickness. In this book, ggplot size adjustments are done separately from the R code (via Quarto chunk options). There are various ways to adjust the figure sizes in different environments.









WarningAvoid giant bars



Some libraries have a fixed chart size and expand the space allocated to categories to fill the entire chart instead of allocating a fixed space per category. This can lead to giant bars (and other marks), particularly when there are few categories, as in the figure below. Excessively thick bars can make a chart feel crowded. Adjusting the overall figure size can make the bars narrower.

















WarningAvoid bar charts for means and medians



Remember that the length of the bar suggests that we started at zero and added something up, such as a count or sum. Using bars for means has also been observed to bias viewers toward thinking that individual observations are more likely to fall within the graphical region of the bar than beyond it, even at equal distances from the mean.1



Sorting groups

In our chart above, the groups on the y-axis are sorted in alphabetical order. Sorting by count instead makes it easier to compare groups with similar counts and identify those with the most and fewest observations.

Altairggplot


The sort() method takes the name of another visual channel to sort by, such as 'x', 'color', etc.

alt.Chart(meditation).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()',
    y=alt.Y('condition').sort('x')
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




This places the largest bar at the bottom, nearest the x-axis. To place it at the top instead, pass '-x' rather than 'x'. Either direction can work, but generally it is more visually appealing to have the longest bar, the closest to the axis.


The base R function reorder() sets the order of categorical levels based on another column in the dataframe, for example, reorder(column_to_sort, column_to_use_as_sorting_order). To order the categories by their counts, we first need to calculate those counts and add them to the dataframe. Here, we use dplyr::add_count() to create a column automatically named n, then use it to order the categories on the y-axis.

meditation |>
    dplyr::add_count(condition) |>
    ggplot(aes(y = reorder(condition, -n))) +
        geom_bar()








We used -n to put the longest bar the closest to the axis. To put the largest count at the top instead, use reorder(condition, n). Either direction can work; but generally it is more visually appealing to have the longest bar, the closest to the axis.



Ordering categories by their plotted values can also help in other charts, such as point charts of group means. However, when categories have a meaningful order, such as education levels or days of the week, preserving that order is generally more useful than sorting by value. Here, there is no such natural order, but we show an example of how we would define one.

Altairggplot


The custom order is passed to sort, just as when ordering by another visual channel.

custom_order = ['Control (book chapter)', 'Mindful breathing', 'Body scan', 'Mindful walking', 'Loving kindness']
alt.Chart(meditation).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()',
    y=alt.Y('condition').sort(custom_order)
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






When ordering by another visual channel we used reorder to change the order of the dataframe column. To define a custom order, we need to directly manipulate order of the scale that the categorical variable is plotting on, in this case the y scale.

custom_order <- c('Control (book chapter)', 'Mindful breathing', 'Body scan', 'Mindful walking', 'Loving kindness')
ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition)) +
    geom_bar() +
    scale_y_discrete(limits = custom_order)














Stacked bars
Like area charts, bar charts can also show multiple groups as segments stacked on top of each other. Let’s explore this in the following exercise:






Ex-promptExercise 1






For example, we might be interested in how participants’ self-reported gender is distributed across the study conditions.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(meditation).mark_bar().encode(
    y='condition',
    x='count()',
    color='gender'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition, fill = gender)) +
    geom_bar()











In this chart, it is easy to see that all conditions have more female than male respondents. Is it equally easy to identify which conditions have the most male and female participants? Why, and how could we make the harder comparison easier?






Ex-hintHint






Look at which bar segments start at zero and which start at another segment’s endpoint. The difficulty is the same as for stacked areas. But the solution is slightly different since we have more options than just layering the bars on top of each other.






Ex-solutionSolution






It is difficult to compare counts when the corresponding bar segments do not share a common baseline. This means that we are left trying to mentally align the bars to compare their lengths in our mind. This is much harder than reading the endpoints against a shared x-axis baseline.
We could switch to a point mark, just as we switched from areas to lines to solve a similar problem, but bars also offer a useful alternative: we can put them next to each other within each condition.

Altairggplot


The yOffset/xOffset encodings that we used for jittering can also take a categorical variable to offset groups next to each other.

alt.Chart(meditation).mark_bar().encode(
    y='condition',
    x='count()',
    color='gender',
    yOffset='gender'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  






The position parameter that we used for jittering can also take the 'dodge' value, which places bars next to one another instead of stacking them.

ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition, fill = gender)) +
    geom_bar(position = 'dodge')











Now both gender categories can be compared across conditions using a shared zero baseline. Body scan and mindful breathing tie for the most male participants, with 36 each; the control condition has the most female participants, with 86.


















WarningAvoid stacked bar charts when exact group comparisons matter



As with stacked areas, it is difficult to compare the bar segments that do not share a baseline, since we have to rely on their length rather than aligned endpoint positions. Stacked bars work best when the total, such as the count per condition, is of primary importance and precise comparisons between segments are of secondary importance.

title: 8  Counts & proportions
text:
8.2 Proportions
A proportion expresses a part relative to a whole. For categorical counts, we calculate it by dividing the count for a subgroup by the total count for the relevant group; multiplying by 100 gives a percentage. Here, each condition is the whole, and the gender categories are its parts. Normalizing each bar to the same length lets us compare gender proportions even though the conditions have different numbers of participants.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(meditation).mark_bar().encode(
    y='condition',
    x=alt.X('count()').stack('normalize'),
    color='gender'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




We could change the displayed axis values from percentages to proportions by formatting the axis labels as decimals with one digit after the decimal point (.1f). Here, labelExpr formats each tick value directly, overriding the default percentage labels:

alt.Chart(meditation).mark_bar().encode(
    y='condition',
    x=alt.X('count()')
    .stack('normalize')
    .axis(labelExpr=alt.expr.format(alt.datum.value, '.1f')),
    color='gender'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition, fill = gender)) +
    geom_bar(position = 'fill')








We could change the displayed axis values from proportions to percentages by specifying that the scale labels are percentages:

ggplot(meditation, aes(y = condition, fill = gender)) +
    geom_bar(position = 'fill') +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent())











With two segments in each normalized bar, both proportions can be compared against a shared reference: one segment starts at zero, and the other ends at one (100%). With three or more segments, those in the middle generally lack an aligned endpoint, making them harder to compare. Proportions can also be shown with side-by-side bars sharing a zero baseline.
Always make the denominator clear. These bars show proportions within each condition, not proportions of the whole sample. Normalizing also hides differences in sample size: the conditions contain between 84 and 113 participants, but all five normalized bars have the same total length. Across the complete 500-observation sample, 344 participants reported female gender (68.8%).

Pie charts
Pie charts use angles and areas to indicate magnitude. They should generally be avoided as bar charts with a shared baseline tend to communicate the same insights more effectively. A minor point in favor of pie charts is that familiar fractions, such as one-quarter and one-half, can be easy to recognize. They can therefore be useful for illustration and simple comparisons with just two or (maybe) three groups.

Altairggplot


theta is the visual channel that controls the angle of each slice in the pie.

alt.Chart(meditation).mark_arc().encode(
    theta=alt.Theta('count()').stack(True),
    color='gender'
)




  
  
  
  
  


  
  




We can also adjust the inner and outer radii. Setting an inner radius greater than zero creates a donut chart.


In ggplot, we can construct a pie chart by transforming a stacked bar into polar coordinates with coord_polar(); a very grammatically coherent way to express a pie chart!

ggplot(meditation, aes(x = factor(1), fill = gender)) +
    geom_bar() +
    coord_polar(theta = 'y')

















WarningAvoid pie charts for precise comparisons



It is almost always better to use some form of a bar chart. When there are many groups in the data, pie charts can be disorienting. The charts below show parliamentary seats from the 2026 Swedish election.2, with parties grouped into their blocs from last election. In the bar chart to the left, it is easier to see that Bloc 1 has slightly more seats: 176 compared with 173, and we could make this even clearer by adding a line/rule at the majority cutoff or by making the figure larger. In the middle pie chart, comparing the bloc totals is much harder because each bloc is split across several party slices. Even in the simplified rightmost pie chart which shows only the seats per bloc, the small difference between the two slices is difficult to judge.





  
  
  
  
  


  
  







Another way of thinking of these count charts is that we are viewing distributions of categorical values. This concept can also be applied to quantitative values, as we will see in Chapter 9.

title: 8  Counts & proportions
text:
Bar graphs depicting averages are perceptually misinterpreted: The within-the-bar bias↩︎
Source: Swedish Election Authority, final results for 2026↩︎

title: 9  Binned distributions
text:
9.1 Why bother?
In Chapter 7, we learned that it is important to inspect the underlying observations to see how they are distributed. Much of that information would be hidden if we looked only at a summary like the mean or median. But what happens when we have too many data points to visualize all of them individually?

title: 9  Binned distributions
text:
Ex-promptExercise 1






In this chart, there are so many observations that the plot is saturated and it is difficult to tell how the data points are distributed. How do you think we could plot the observations to more clearly see how they are distributed?





  
  
  
  
  


  
  










Ex-hintHint






We could, of course, increase the size of the chart to jitter the points more, but it would still be difficult to get an overall idea of how the observations are distributed. What if we could use what we learned in the previous chapter about counting to help us here?






Ex-solutionSolution






Instead of showing each individual observation, we could visualize the counts of observations within intervals (or “bins”) of the quantitative variable on the x-axis. Conceptually, we could think of this as first creating bins along the x-axis (for example, one bin could include runtimes from 80 up to, but not including, 100 minutes), then counting all the observations that fall within each bin, and finally drawing a bar with a height corresponding to the count of observations. This type of chart is called a histogram.

title: 9  Binned distributions
text:
9.2 How to create histograms
The histogram creation process we described above can be viewed in this animated schematic:






Figure 9.1: Animated schematic of creating a histogram



Binning is useful because observations of a continuous or finely measured variable may rarely have exactly the same value. Counting each distinct value separately can produce a spiky, sparse chart. Grouping nearby values into intervals helps us see broader patterns.
We could create the intervals manually in the dataframe and plot a categorical count chart as in the previous chapter, but there is a special type of chart to help us create the bins and counts for a quantitative variable: the histogram.
Let’s create a histogram for the entire dataset first, before breaking it down into the different movie genres.

Altairggplot


VegaFusion makes it easier to work with large datasets in Altair by precomputing supported data transformations in Python. Altair’s default data transformer limits inline datasets to 5,000 rows; VegaFusion is one way to work with larger datasets, such as the marathon example later in this chapter. It also works with smaller datasets (read more about VegaFusion in the Altair documentation).

import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

alt.data_transformers.enable('vegafusion')

DataTransformerRegistry.enable('vegafusion')


We can use the bin() method on the alt.X or alt.Y helper class to divide the quantitative variable into intervals along that axis. A distribution chart that is wider than it is tall is often more visually appealing and can make the distribution shape easier to follow, so we use a compact chart height here.

movies = pd.read_csv('data/movies.csv')
alt.Chart(movies, height=150).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min').bin(),
    y='count()',
)




  
  
  
  


  
  




The small gaps between the bars make it easier to distinguish individual bins. If we wanted to, we could show the histogram as one connected graphical unit, which can sometimes make it less messy to compare multiple histograms in the same chart.

alt.Chart(movies, height=150).mark_bar(binSpacing=0).encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min').bin(),
    y='count()',
)




  
  
  
  


  
  






We can use stat = 'bin' to divide the quantitative variable into intervals and count the observations in each one. A chart that is wider than it is tall can make the distribution easy to follow, so this chapter uses a compact default figure height.

library(ggplot2)

movies <- readr::read_csv('data/movies.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)
ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`)) +
    geom_bar(stat = 'bin')








As a shortcut for geom_bar(stat = 'bin'), we could use geom_histogram(), which we will do from now on.
Showing the histogram as one connected graphical unit, as above, can sometimes make it less cluttered to compare multiple histograms in the same chart, but separating the bars makes it easier to distinguish individual bins. Here, adding color = 'white' draws white outlines around the bars, creating the appearance of gaps between them without changing the bin boundaries.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`)) +
    geom_histogram(color = 'white')











Histograms make counts within intervals explicit and they are easy to understand and explain, but their appearance depends heavily on how we choose those intervals.

title: 9  Binned distributions
text:
9.3 Bin properties
The bin width controls how much detail we can see. Narrow bins separate nearby values and can reveal small concentrations or gaps, but they can also emphasize incidental variation. Wide bins combine more observations and emphasize broad patterns, but they can hide important features. Let’s see how we can configure the bin width to be more narrow and reveal more details from the distribution.

Altairggplot


To show more detail, reduce the step of each bin to 5 so that each bin now spans five minutes:

alt.Chart(movies, height=150).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min').bin(step=5),
    y='count()',
)




  
  
  
  


  
  






To show more detail, reduce the binwidth of each bin to 5 so that each bin now spans five minutes:

ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, color = 'white')











If no bin width is set, visualization libraries have different rules of thumb try to determine a suitable width. Libraries also tend to make different decisions around whether bins should favor round-number boundaries and regarding how axis labels and bins should align. Regardless of which library you use, it is a good idea to try several settings as different features of the distribution can stand out at different bin widths. When doing so, it is helpful to think about the variable’s units, the question you want to answer, and whether aligning width to round numbers are important to make the chart easier to interpret.






Ex-promptExercise 2






To experience the impact of different bin widths, we explore a dataset containing finish times from the 2023 London Marathon for male runners aged 18–39. Use the slider to explore different bin widths in the histogram. Which bin width would you choose? And how would you explain the peaks that become visible when the bins are narrower?





  
  
  
  


  
  




You can hover over a bar to see its interval and count. Note that the count-axis varies as the bin-width changes, why do you think this is?






Ex-hintHint






It seems like the peaks are just before the round numbers 180, 210, and 240 min. How many hours do these minute values correspond to?






Ex-solutionSolution






In this case, the peaks are not a binning artefact or technical noise; they reflect a real phenomena in the underlying data. These concentrations in finish times occur just before round-numbers, consistent with runners aiming to finish below a target time. Popular targets include 3 hours, 3 hours 30 minutes, and 4 hours, which correspond to 180, 210, and 240 minutes.1 Trying several bin widths helps us check whether these concentrations persist rather than trusting a peak that appears with only one binning choice.
The y-axis labels show lower count number for narrower bins, since less runners fit within each bin. Note that a lower count per bin does not imply a less concentrated distribution, just that we have distributed the counts across more individual bins within the same interval.


















WarningAvoid looking at just a single histogram



Various attributes of the distribution can stand out at different bin widths. It is therefore important to try a few different bin widths and reflect on which features of the underlying data they might highlight.


Bin width is not the only choice that affects a histogram’s appearance. Even histograms with the same bin width can look quite different when their boundaries are shifted along the x-axis. In Figure 9.2, we can see that the left histogram seems to show a long-tailed distribution, but when the bins are shifted over in the rightmost histogram, it now looks like a potentially bimodal distribution with two peaks.







  
  
  
  


  
  



Figure 9.2: The same data has been used to create these two histograms, which also share a bin width of 50 units. The only difference is that the start and end points of the bins are shifted slightly between the two charts. This figure is just for illustrative purposes, so we have kept the variable name off the axes.

title: 9  Binned distributions
text:
9.4 Adding back individual observations
The histogram shortcomings we have learned about can be somewhat alleviated by showing individual observations alongside the histogram. We can use jittered points, as at the start of the chapter, or we can use a small tick to mark each observation in what is often called a “rug” plot. We have already covered the downsides of visualizing all individual observations, such as overlap that can saturate the chart. Even so, individual marks often complement a histogram well.

Altairggplot


We create the tick mark as a separate chart that we then concatenate vertically with the histogram using the operator &. We also indicate that the scale of the x-axes should be shared between the two charts so that the ticks align with the histogram and it is easy to see which observations belong to which bin.

hist = alt.Chart(movies, height=150).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min').bin(step=10),
    y='count()',
)

rug = alt.Chart(movies).mark_tick().encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min'),
)

(hist & rug).resolve_scale(x='shared')




  
  
  
  


  
  






We could have created a separate chart with the individual observations that we concatenated vertically with the histogram. But there is also geom_rug(), which makes this a bit more convenient by plotting the individual observations directly in the margin of the canvas.

ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`)) +
    geom_histogram(color = 'white') +
    geom_rug()

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.

title: 9  Binned distributions
text:
9.5 Multiple distributions
With all that we have learned about histograms in mind, let’s finally create a version of the plot we started this chapter with, using histograms rather than jittered points.






WarningAvoid too many histograms in the same chart



You might be tempted to simply group the histograms using color in the same chart, but it easily becomes difficult to separate the histograms visually so it is not an effective way to visualize distributions, as you can see in this chart.


Altairggplot


Since bars stack on top of each other by default, we need to set stack(False) on the y-axis, so that they all share a common baseline. To be able to see the bars behind each other, we make them partially transparent by setting opacity=0.5.

alt.Chart(movies, height=150).mark_bar(opacity=0.5).encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min').bin(step=5),
    y=alt.Y('count()').stack(False),
    color='Major Genre',
)




  
  
  
  


  
  






Since bars stack on top of each other by default, we need to set position = 'identity', so that they all share a common baseline. To be able to see the bars behind each other, we make them partially transparent with the alpha parameter.

ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`, fill = `Major Genre`)) +
    geom_histogram(color = 'white', position = 'identity', alpha = 0.5)

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.












One exception to this rule is if the distributions are well-separated along the axis, or there are only two (or maybe three) distributions in the chart; then a colored histogram chart can be effective.





  
  
  
  


  
  






A more effective way to visualize multiple distributions as histograms is to place each movie genre in a separate facet. Since we are interested in comparing the distributions across genres, we create all facets in a single column, which aligns their x-axes and facilitates seeing shifts in the distributions between genres. Use the same bin boundaries and axis scales across facets to make those comparisons meaningful.

Altairggplot



alt.Chart(movies, height=80).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('Running Time min').bin(step=5),
    y='count()',
).facet(
    'Major Genre',
    columns=1
)




  
  
  
  


  
  







ggplot(movies, aes(x = `Running Time min`)) +
    geom_histogram(color = 'white') +
    facet_wrap(vars(`Major Genre`), ncol = 1)

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.












Now we can detect differences that we couldn’t see in the original jittered point plot. For example, adventure movies span a broad range of runtimes, whereas comedies tend to be more tightly concentrated.
